venues.a: Srinagar (Gupkar / palace grounds, above Dal Lake)
venues.d: The Maharaja's own palace, set in 101 acres of chinar-shaded gardens above the Dal — the grandest address in the valley.

venues.a: Srinagar (Kralsangri, Brein — Zabarwan hillside above Dal Lake)
venues.d: The Taj flagship of the valley, set high on the Zabarwan hills with the Dal, the Mughal gardens and the Pir Panjal laid out below.

venues.n: The Khyber Himalayan Resort & Spa, Gulmarg
venues.d: A timber-and-stone lodge at 8,825 ft in the Pir Panjal, facing the snows of Apharwat — the finest mountain address in Kashmir.

venues.a: Srinagar (western Dal Lake, by the Mughal 'Garden of the Morning Breeze')
venues.d: The most storied houseboats on the Dal — moored under century-old chinars, where George Harrison learned sitar with Ravi Shankar.
The Dal Lake houseboat reimagined — carved walnut and cream linen, a rooftop terrace and a level of service found nowhere else on the water.

venues.n: Vivanta Dal View — Boulevard heritage stays
venues.d: The dependable, well-run polish of a global group on the Dal's edge, minutes from the gardens and the shikara ghats.

venues.n: The Chinar at The Lalit Grand Palace
venues.d: The grand Wazwan, served in the Maharaja's palace with the gardens and Dal beyond — the most refined Kashmiri feast in the city.
The century-old benchmark of Kashmiri cooking — Persian carpets, old Srinagar photographs, and Wazwan as it should be.
A city institution for the full spread — Wazwan-e-Khas and the finest cuts, done with real skill and no fuss.
Authentic Kashmiri cooking a step from the Dal — Tabak Maaz, seekh kebabs and Rogan Josh with the lake at the door.
The valley's beloved pure-vegetarian institution — jam-packed, unpretentious, and famous for its dal makhani.

venues.n: A Shikara Ride on Dal Lake
venues.d: The slow, cushioned glide of a hand-paddled shikara through the still water at golden hour is the image of Kashmir every Indian carries in their head. Have a private boat held for the family at first light or last light, when the lake empties of day-trippers and the Zabarwan hills turn copper on the surface.

The carved-cedar houseboats moored on the Dal and the quieter Nagin are a living relic of the Raj, all fretwork panelling, Kashmiri carpets and a verandah that opens straight onto the water. Book a full boat for the family for a night or two as a set-piece, then move to a hotel like the Vivanta or Lalit for the comforts a longer stay wants.

venues.n: The Floating Vegetable Market at Dawn
venues.d: Before sunrise, growers from the lake's floating gardens gather in a knot of shikaras to trade lotus stems, greens and haakh, bargaining boat-to-boat on the black water. It is the one experience here that rewards an unglamorous alarm; a guide who knows the growers gets you into the ring rather than watching from the edge.

A tiny island in the Dal marked by four great chinar trees at its corners, laid out by a Mughal prince and unchanged in feel for centuries. Paddle out by shikara for kahwa under the plane trees, with the whole amphitheatre of lake, houseboats and mountains around you.

The Dal's clearer, quieter sister, ringed by willows and the calmest houseboats in the valley. Families who want the Dal's romance without its bustle base themselves here; the swimming and the stillness make it the connoisseur's address in Srinagar.

Jahangir's garden of love, built in 1619 for the empress Nur Jahan, its central water channel stepping down through terraces of chinar shade to the Dal below. It is the grandest of the Mughal gardens and the one that most fully explains why the emperors called Kashmir paradise.

The 'garden of gladness', a twelve-terraced sweep on the eastern shore of the Dal, laid out in 1633 with the Zabarwan range rising directly behind it and the lake spread out in front. The most dramatically sited of all the gardens; go late afternoon when the light rakes across the terraces.

The smallest and most intimate of the Mughal gardens, built around a natural spring whose cold, sweet water is still bottled and carried home by Kashmiris for its reputed purity. A short, gentle visit with a fine view down over the Dal, easily paired with the tulip garden and Pari Mahal just above.

The terraced 'palace of the fairies', a former Sufi library and observatory cut into the mountainside above Chashme Shahi, with the finest single view in Srinagar: the whole Dal, the city and the encircling hills laid out below. Come as the light goes and the lamps of the city begin to answer the last of the sun.

A grove of some 700 towering chinar trees planted by the Mughals on the Dal's shore, now within the university campus and largely free of crowds. Walking its cathedral of plane trees, especially when they burn red in autumn, is the quiet, knowing counterpoint to the famous gardens.

Kashmir's holiest Muslim shrine, its white marble dome mirrored in the Dal on the lake's western shore, home to the Moi-e-Muqaddas relic revered across the valley. Even for non-Muslim visitors it is a moving, deeply local place; dress modestly and go with a guide who can read its significance.

Srinagar's great congregational mosque, first built in the 14th century, its vast prayer hall carried on more than 370 deodar pillars around a still courtyard. The wooden Indo-Saracenic architecture is unlike any mosque elsewhere in India and the anchor of any walk through the old city.

The valley's oldest and most beautiful Sufi shrine, a river-side confection of carved and painted woodwork, papier-mache ceilings and hanging lamps built where Kashmir's Islam first took root. Non-Muslims view from the exterior and threshold; the craftsmanship alone justifies the stop.

An ancient Shiva temple crowning a hill above the city, reached by a long stair or a drive, and named for the philosopher Adi Shankara who is said to have meditated here. The 360-degree view over Srinagar and the Dal is the reward; go early before the haze and the crowds.

The Afghan-era fort crowns a hill sacred to all three of Kashmir's faiths, ringed by the Sharika Devi temple, the Makhdoom Sahib Sufi shrine and a gurudwara on its slopes. A short, layered pilgrimage that captures the syncretic soul of old Srinagar in one climb.

The valley's principal museum, founded in 1898, with tens of thousands of objects: Kashmiri shawls and papier-mache, ancient sculpture, coins and Gandhara-era pieces. An hour here gives the crafts you will see in the bazaars their proper historical depth.

The multi-course royal Kashmiri banquet — rista, rogan josh, gushtaba and the rest, traditionally up to thirty-six dishes served on the shared copper trami — is the region's great table ritual, honed over generations of master wazas. Arrange a proper hosted Wazwan (a substantial vegetarian version can be laid on) as the centrepiece meal of the trip.

The saffron-and-almond green tea called kahwa, poured from a samovar against the cold, and the morning kandur bakeries with their salt-tea breads — girda, lavasa, sheermal — are the small daily rituals that define Kashmiri hospitality. A guide can walk you into a working bakery at dawn, tea glass in hand.

The genuine article — hand-spun pashm woven on a Kashmiri loom, or the intricate Kani shawl worked stitch-by-stitch on wooden spokes — is one of the finest textiles on earth and an heirloom purchase. Buy only through a trusted, GI-verified house; a private guide keeps you clear of the machine-made pretenders that flood the market.

Hand-knotted silk and wool carpets in Persian-derived patterns, and the chain-stitched crewel and namda work that dresses Kashmiri homes, are among the valley's signature crafts. The best ateliers will show you the knot count and the design cards; a considered carpet is the trip's grandest souvenir.

For a few weeks from mid-March to April, seven terraces below the Zabarwan range blaze with well over a million tulips in scores of colours, framed by the Dal below. It opens for the annual Tulip Festival; time a spring trip to it and little else in the valley compares.

In February and early March, before anything else in the valley stirs, this historic almond garden at the foot of Hari Parbat breaks into pink-and-white blossom — Kashmir's first sign of spring. A quiet, uncrowded pleasure that most itineraries miss entirely.

A Robert Trent Jones Jr. course laid along the slopes above the Dal, consistently rated among India's very best and one of the most scenic in Asia. A round here, chinars and lake below and snow peaks beyond, is a rare thing to do on a Kashmir morning.

The two-stage cable car climbs from the Gulmarg meadow to nearly 4,000 metres on the shoulder of Apharwat Peak, one of the highest passenger ropeways in the world with a Himalayan panorama at the top. Do both phases on a clear morning; carry warm layers even in summer, as it is another world up there.

The 'meadow of flowers' is a vast bowl of alpine grass ringed by the Pir Panjal, and in summer its greens make up the highest golf course in the world. An easy, glorious day-trip base from Srinagar for families, with pony rides, walks and views in every direction.

In winter Gulmarg becomes one of Asia's serious ski destinations, with genuine high-altitude powder off Apharwat reached by the gondola, plus gentle nursery slopes for first-timers and children. Arrange instructors and gear in advance; the off-piste here draws skiers from around the world.

The 'valley of shepherds' sits where the glacier-fed Lidder river runs cold and clear through pine and meadow, the classic Kashmiri summer retreat two-and-a-half hours from Srinagar. It makes a superb overnight base — riverside luxury stays, gentle walks and cool air — for families escaping the plains' heat.

A wide green bowl where pine forests meet the Lidder, named for the Bollywood film shot here and postcard-perfect in every direction. An easy, level, kid-friendly stop that delivers the archetypal Kashmir meadow with almost no walking.

A hushed hamlet and meadow upriver from Pahalgam, the trailhead for the Kolahoi glacier and the Tarsar–Marsar lakes and far quieter than the main town. The place to base for a day of gentle riverside walks or a serious trek with a private outfitter.

The end of the motorable road up the Lidder, where snow lingers into summer and the annual Amarnath pilgrimage traditionally sets off on foot. A scenic drive to a high, cold, dramatic spot with a taste of the sacred geography beyond.

'Meadow of gold', a high alpine bowl at around 2,700 metres on the road to Ladakh, where the Sindh river braids through grass under snow-streaked peaks. The most alpine-feeling of the valley's day-trips and the classic launch point for river rafting and pony rides.

A short pony ride or walk from Sonamarg brings you to the snout of the Thajiwas glacier, ringed by conifers and meadows and holding snow through much of the year. A rare chance to stand at a glacier with children in tow, no serious trekking required.

A quiet, rolling meadow of pines and open grass south-west of Srinagar that the crowds still largely skip, its name meaning 'meadow of Jesus'. The hidden-gem alternative to Gulmarg for a family picnic day, all space and silence and horse rides.

The 'valley of milk', an emerald meadow laced by a shallow, milk-white stream about an hour and a half from Srinagar, still one of Kashmir's least-spoilt escapes. Come for a slow, uncrowded day on the grass — the antidote to the well-trodden circuit.

The deepest lake in Kashmir, an hour north of the city, quiet and mirror-still with lotus blooming across it in summer and a small Mughal garden on its shore. A serene, birdwatcher's day-trip almost no tourist itinerary bothers with.

One of the largest freshwater lakes in Asia, fed by the Jhelum and fringed by the villages of north Kashmir, vast and thinly visited. A guided trip out here — birdlife, fishing hamlets, open water under the mountains — is for travellers who have already done the classics.

The deep, octagonal Mughal-walled spring that is the chief source of the Jhelum, ringed by chinars and remarkably peaceful, south of Srinagar on the Pahalgam road. A worthwhile detour that completes the story of the Mughals' love affair with Kashmir's water.

A serene Mughal spring-garden laid out for Nur Jahan around a powerful natural spring, with cascades, chinar avenues and far fewer visitors than the Srinagar gardens. A graceful, unhurried stop that pairs naturally with a run down towards Pahalgam.

The plateau around Pampore, minutes outside Srinagar, grows the world-renowned Kashmiri saffron, and for a fortnight each late autumn the fields turn purple with crocus at harvest. A short, vivid seasonal detour — and the place to buy the real, GI-tagged spice at source.

A protected valley half an hour from the city and the last refuge of the endangered hangul, the Kashmir stag, alongside black bears and leopards in wooded slopes above the Dal. A permitted, guided visit is a rare wildlife dimension to a trip most people spend entirely on lakes and gardens.

Past the grand banquet lies an everyday table worth exploring — haakh greens, nadru (lotus stem), morel mushrooms, the sour-red mujj chetin, and the lake's own fish — much of it deeply vegetarian-friendly. A guided food morning, from bakery to tea-house to home kitchen, is its own small journey.

For a few weeks in late October and November the valley's chinars turn crimson and gold — Naseem Bagh, the Mughal gardens, the university, whole avenues ablaze — in what Kashmiris call the harud. The quietest, most photogenic and most underrated time to come.
The valley's true night out — kahwa and dinner on your own carved-walnut deck as the lake goes silent and the hills fade to dark.
